n5_g001.explanation: Used to state facts about the topic. は (wa) marks the topic of the sentence. です (desu) is a polite sentence-ending that means 'is/am/are'.

n5_g002.meaning: Negative form of です (is not)
n5_g002.explanation: The negative of 〜です. In casual speech, じゃないです or じゃありません can also be used.

n5_g003.meaning: Subject marker が — marks the subject performing the action
n5_g003.explanation: が marks the grammatical subject. Unlike は which marks the topic, が focuses on who/what performs the action or has the quality.
n5_g003.example: I like cats. (Cats are what I like.)

n5_g004.meaning: Object marker を — marks the direct object of a transitive verb
n5_g004.explanation: を (pronounced 'o') marks the direct object — the thing that receives the action of a transitive verb.

n5_g005.meaning: Existence: there is/are (あります for inanimate, います for animate)
n5_g005.explanation: Use あります for non-living things and います for living things (people, animals). The location is marked with に.
n5_g005.example: There is a book on the desk.

n5_g006.meaning: で marks location of action OR means/method
n5_g006.explanation: で has two key uses: (1) marks where an action takes place, (2) marks the means or tool used to do something.

n5_g007.meaning: Direction marker に with movement verbs (go/come/return to)
n5_g007.explanation: に marks the destination with verbs of movement like 行く (go), 来る (come), 帰る (return). The particle へ can also be used interchangeably in most cases.

n5_g008.explanation: Attach たい to the verb stem (remove ます from masu-form). The result is treated like an い-adjective. Negative: たくないです. Past: たかったです.
n5_g008.example: I want to go to Japan.

n5_g009.meaning: Let's do ~ (making a suggestion or invitation)
n5_g009.explanation: ましょう is the volitional/hortative form. It suggests doing something together. ましょうか is softer: 'Shall we?'

n5_g010.explanation: Form the て-form of the verb and add ください. This is a standard polite way to make requests.

n5_g011.meaning: Currently doing ~ OR state resulting from action
n5_g011.explanation: Two main uses: (1) ongoing action — I am doing something right now; (2) resultant state — a state that results from a completed action (married, know, wearing).
n5_g011.example: I am reading a book now.

n5_g012.explanation: The た-form indicates completed actions. For polite speech, use ました. For plain/casual speech, use た directly.

n5_g013.explanation: Attach ないで to the nai-form (negative plain form) of a verb, then add ください. Used to politely ask someone not to do something.

n5_g014.explanation: から marks the starting point and まで marks the end point. Can be used with time (9 o'clock to 5) or place (Tokyo to Osaka).

n5_g015.explanation: も replaces は, が, or を to mean 'also' or 'too'. When used with negatives it means 'neither/either': 〜もありません.

n5_g016.explanation: の connects two nouns, showing possession (my book), origin (Japanese music), or description (coffee shop). The modifier always comes before の.

n5_g017.explanation: や lists examples from a larger group (implying 'and things like these'). など adds 'etc.' or 'and so on'. Contrast with と which lists everything exhaustively.
n5_g017.example: I bought fruits, vegetables, and so on.

n5_g018.explanation: と has three uses: (1) lists nouns exhaustively (A and B, nothing else), (2) marks a companion (with someone), (3) marks a quotation or thought before 言う/思う.
n5_g018.example: I ate an apple and a mandarin orange.

n5_g019.meaning: ね = seeking agreement / よ = asserting information
n5_g019.explanation: ね is used when you expect the listener to agree or share the same feeling. よ asserts information the listener may not know. よね combines both.

n5_g020.explanation: か at the end of a sentence makes it a question. In polite speech (〜ますか、〜ですか) the intonation stays flat. In casual speech, just raise the intonation.

n5_g021.explanation: Indicates that one action is completed before the next begins. The て-form + から emphasises that the first action is fully done before the second starts.
n5_g021.example: After washing my hands, I eat.

n5_g022.meaning: Do things like ~ and ~ (non-exhaustive list of actions)
n5_g022.explanation: Lists representative activities without implying it's a complete list. Form: change verb to た-form, add り, repeat for other verbs, end with します.
n5_g022.example: On weekends I do things like watch movies and listen to music.

n5_g023.meaning: Can do ~ / be able to do ~ (ability or possibility)
n5_g023.explanation: Expresses ability or possibility. The simpler alternative is the potential verb form (食べられる). ことができる is slightly more formal.

n5_g024.explanation: 前に with a verb (dictionary form) means 'before doing'. With a noun, use の前に. The action in 前に clause is not yet completed.
n5_g024.example: I brush my teeth before sleeping.

n5_g025.explanation: 後で indicates an action happens after another. With verbs, use the た-form. With nouns, use の後で.
n5_g025.example: After class ends, I will go to the library.

n5_g026.meaning: い-adjective: negative, past, and negative past forms
n5_g026.explanation: い-adjectives conjugate by changing the final い: drop い and add くない (neg), かった (past), くなかった (neg past). Exception: いい → よい → よくない / よかった.

n5_g027.meaning: な-adjective: negative, past, and negative past forms
n5_g027.explanation: な-adjectives conjugate like nouns + です. Negative: じゃありません/ではありません. Past: でした. Neg past: じゃありませんでした.

n5_g028.explanation: より marks the standard of comparison (A). のほうが marks what is being compared favourably (B). The adjective follows.
n5_g028.example: I like cats more than dogs.

n5_g029.meaning: ~ is the most / ~ is number one (superlative)
n5_g029.explanation: 一番 (いちばん) means 'number one' or 'most'. Place it before the adjective. To specify the group, use 〜の中で〜が一番.

n5_g030.explanation: から after a clause gives the reason for what follows. In polite speech, both clauses use polite forms. In casual speech, plain forms are used.
n5_g030.example: Because I am sleepy, I will sleep early.

n5_g031.explanation: ので gives a reason like から but sounds more objective and polite. Better for formal situations. な-adjectives and nouns use なので before ので.
n5_g031.example: Since I am tired, I will rest.

n5_g032.explanation: が as a conjunction connects two contrasting clauses like 'but' or 'however'. It can also soften a statement without strong contrast.

n5_g033.explanation: どんな asks about the type or quality of something. Similar to 'what kind of' in English.
n5_g033.example: What kind of music do you like?

n5_g034.explanation: なる means 'to become'. い-adjectives change い to くなる. な-adjectives and nouns use になる.
n5_g034.example: When spring comes, it becomes warm.

n5_g035.meaning: It is okay to ~ / You may ~ (giving or asking permission)
n5_g035.explanation: 〜てもいいです gives permission. 〜てもいいですか asks for permission. To deny: 〜てはいけません or 〜てはだめです.

n5_g036.meaning: Must not ~ / It is not allowed to ~ (prohibition)
n5_g036.explanation: 〜てはいけません prohibits an action. More forceful than 〜ないでください. Common in rules and regulations.

n5_g037.explanation: Expresses obligation. Formed by changing ない to なければ and adding なりません. Casual: 〜なきゃ or 〜なければ.
n5_g037.example: I must wake up early tomorrow.

n5_g038.explanation: Expresses probability or supposition. でしょう is polite; だろう is plain/casual. Often used with たぶん (probably).

n5_g039.meaning: I think that ~ (expressing opinion or belief)
n5_g039.explanation: Used to express the speaker's opinion or belief. The clause before と is always in plain form. と思っています implies ongoing thinking.

n5_g040.meaning: I heard that ~ / They say that ~ (hearsay)
n5_g040.explanation: Reports information heard from others. Always in plain form before そうです. Different from そうです (appearance) which uses verb stem/adj stem.
n5_g040.example: I heard that Mr. Tanaka will get married next month.

n5_g041.explanation: 時 (とき) means 'time' or 'when'. Use verb dictionary form for future/habitual events, た-form for completed events.
n5_g041.example: When I was a child, I often played in the park.

n5_g042.explanation: 毎 (まい) means 'every'. Common forms: 毎日 (every day), 毎週 (every week), 毎月 (every month), 毎年 (every year), 毎朝 (every morning), 毎晩 (every evening).

n5_g043.explanation: ごろ is used for approximate points in time. ぐらい/くらい is used for approximate amounts or durations.

n5_g044.explanation: 番目 makes ordinal numbers. 一番目 (first), 二番目 (second). In some contexts, 番目 is dropped: 一番 (number one/most).

n5_g045.meaning: About ~ / To the extent of ~ (degree or comparison)
n5_g045.explanation: Both express degree or extent. ほど is more formal and also used in comparisons: 〜ほど〜ない (not as ~ as).
n5_g045.example: I was so tired I could die.

n5_g046.explanation: あげる = give (to others), もらう = receive (from others), くれる = give (to me/my group). These determine the direction of giving.
n5_g046.example: I gave a present to my friend.

n5_g047.meaning: Say that ~ / be called ~ (quoting or naming)
n5_g047.explanation: と言います quotes direct or indirect speech. Also used to say what something is called: 〜と言います means 'is called ~'.
n5_g047.example: My name is Tanaka (lit: I am called Tanaka).

n5_g048.meaning: The way of doing ~ / How to do ~
n5_g048.explanation: 方 (かた) attached to a verb stem means 'the way of doing' or 'how to do'. 食べ方 = the way of eating, 書き方 = how to write.
n5_g048.example: Please teach me how to write this kanji.

n5_g049.explanation: すぎる means 'too much' or 'excessively'. Attach to い-adj stem (remove い), な-adj stem, or verb stem (remove ます).

n5_g050.meaning: Easy to do ~ / Hard to do ~ (ease or difficulty)
n5_g050.explanation: やすい means 'easy to do'. にくい means 'hard/difficult to do'. Both attach to the verb stem and conjugate like い-adjectives.
n5_g050.example: This book is easy to read.

n5_g051.meaning: It seems that ~ / It looks like ~ (appearance/inference)
n5_g051.explanation: Both express inference based on observation. ようです is more formal; みたいです is casual. Different from そうです (direct appearance).

n5_g052.explanation: Expresses uncertainty and possibility — lower probability than でしょう. Plain form precedes it; な-adj and nouns drop だ before かもしれません.

n5_g053.explanation: Indicates two actions happening at the same time by the same subject. The main action comes after ながら.
n5_g053.example: I study while listening to music.

n5_g054.meaning: Even ~ / Any ~ (inclusive: even this, any at all)
n5_g054.explanation: でも after a noun means 'even'. After question words (なん、どこ、だれ etc.) it means 'any': なんでも (anything), どこでも (anywhere), だれでも (anyone).
n5_g054.example: It is a book even a child can understand.

n5_g055.meaning: In order to ~ / For the sake of ~ (purpose or benefit)
n5_g055.explanation: ために expresses purpose (in order to do something) or benefit (for someone's sake). Verb form is always dictionary form.
n5_g055.example: In order to study Japanese, I practice every day.

n5_g056.meaning: And ~ and ~ (listing multiple reasons or qualities)
n5_g056.explanation: し lists multiple reasons or qualities, implying 'and also'. Softer than から for giving reasons. Often implies 'among other reasons'.
n5_g056.example: This town is safe, it's clean, and it's easy to live in.

n5_g057.meaning: If ~ / When ~ (conditional: once a condition is met)
n5_g057.explanation: たら expresses a conditional: once A happens, B follows. More natural than と for hypothetical situations. Also used for 'when' in the past: 着いたら電話した (When I arrived, I called).
n5_g057.example: When you finish your homework, let's play.

n5_g058.explanation: Expresses that as one thing increases, another increases proportionally. ば-form + same verb/adj + ほど + result.
n5_g058.example: The more you practice, the better you become.

n5_g059.explanation: だけ limits to only the stated amount or thing. Similar to しか + negative, but だけ has a neutral tone while しか is more emphatic/restrictive.

n5_g060.meaning: Nothing but ~ / Only ~ (with emphasis on insufficiency)
n5_g060.explanation: しか must be followed by a negative verb. Implies the speaker feels the amount is insufficient or surprising. Stronger/more emotional than だけ.
n5_g060.example: I only have 100 yen (and that's not enough).

n4_g001.meaning: Giving/receiving actions (I do for you / you do for me / I receive the favor of)
n4_g001.explanation: あげる: I/someone gives action TO another. くれる: someone gives action TO me. もらう: I receive the action FROM someone.

n4_g002.example: I wish I had studied more.

n4_g003.explanation: Used when you can visually observe that something seems a certain way. Different from the hearsay そうです.

n4_g004.example: It seems Tanaka is not coming.

n4_g005.meaning: It appears that ~ (inference based on observation)

n4_g007.meaning: Maybe ~ / might ~ (possibility, less certain than でしょう)

n4_g008.explanation: Expresses obligation or necessity. Casual forms: なきゃ、なくちゃ. Negative: なくてもいい (don't have to).
n4_g008.example: I must take medicine every day.

n4_g011.example: I have climbed Mt. Fuji before.

n4_g012.meaning: While doing ~ (two simultaneous actions by same person)
n4_g012.example: I study while listening to music.

n4_g014.meaning: In order to ~ / for the purpose of ~
n4_g014.example: I came to Japan in order to learn Japanese.

n4_g015.meaning: So that ~ / in order to ~ (goal/purpose for intransitive verbs)
n4_g015.example: I practice every day so that my Japanese improves.

n3_g001.meaning: It doesn't mean that ~ / It's not that ~
n3_g001.explanation: Used to deny or partially deny an implication. Clarifies a misunderstanding or nuances a statement.
n3_g001.example: It's not that I dislike it, I just don't eat much of it.

n3_g002.example: Despite the rain, the match continued.

n3_g004.meaning: By means of ~ / Depending on ~ / Due to ~
n3_g004.example: This painting was drawn by Picasso.

n3_g007.meaning: If only ~ / As long as ~ (minimum condition)
n3_g007.example: If only I had money, I could buy anything.

n3_g008.meaning: Although ~ / Even though ~ (but the result is unexpected)
n3_g008.example: Although I studied Japanese, I still can't speak it.

n3_g009.example: She can speak not only English but also Japanese.

n3_g010.meaning: Completely finish / Accidentally do / Regrettably do

n3_g011.meaning: It has been decided that ~ / It is expected that ~ (rule/schedule)
n3_g011.example: There is supposed to be a meeting tomorrow.

n3_g012.meaning: There is no way that ~ / Cannot possibly ~
n3_g012.example: There is no way he would say such a thing.

n3_g013.meaning: Just about to ~ / In the middle of ~ / Just finished ~
n3_g013.explanation: Dictionary form + ところ = about to do. ている + ところ = in the middle of doing. た + ところ = just finished doing.
n3_g013.example: I am about to go out now.

n3_g014.example: Along with the changes of the era, technology also advanced.

n3_g015.meaning: In addition to ~ / On top of ~
n3_g015.example: In addition to rain, the wind was also strong.

n2g001.meaning: Despite / in spite of / regardless of
n2g001.explanation: Used to express that something happened contrary to what was expected. Similar to のに but more formal.
n2g001.example: Despite the rain, the game was held.

n2g002.explanation: Used to give an example as a representative of a larger group.
n2g002.example: It will be sold in many cities including Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya.

n2g003.explanation: Adds something extra on top of what was already mentioned.
n2g003.example: In addition to English, I can also speak Japanese.

n2g004.meaning: Might possibly (undesirable result); cannot be ruled out
n2g004.explanation: Expresses concern that something undesirable might happen.
n2g004.example: If left like this, it could possibly lead to a serious accident.

n2g005.explanation: Used when multiple parties have differing views or conflicts about a topic.
n2g005.example: A heated debate took place over the budget.

n2g006.meaning: At the time of / on the occasion of / when doing
n2g006.explanation: Used for important, formal, or special occasions. More formal than〜とき.
n2g006.example: At the time of enrollment, parental consent is required.

n2g007.meaning: Contrary to / against / in opposition to
n2g007.explanation: Indicates that something goes against an expectation, rule, or wish.
n2g007.example: Contrary to expectations, the exam was easy.

n2g008.explanation: Expresses a medium or method by which something is done, or indicates throughout a period.

n2g009.meaning: After (a long process) / at the end of
n2g009.explanation: Used to express something that occurred after a long period of effort or deliberation.
n2g009.example: After a long discussion, a conclusion was reached.

n2g010.explanation: Describes something that extends across a range of time, distance, or area.
n2g010.example: The conference continued for three days.

n2g011.meaning: Toward / against / in contrast to / regarding
n2g011.explanation: Can express direction of action/feeling, contrast, or response toward something.
n2g011.example: He took a rude attitude toward the teacher.

n2g012.explanation: Used to correct or refine a description, suggesting B is more accurate than A.
n2g012.example: Rather than angry, he is sad.

n2g013.meaning: In order to / after doing / in terms of / when it comes to
n2g013.explanation: Used to express a prerequisite action or a consideration in a certain context.
n2g013.example: There are points to be careful of when signing a contract.

n2g014.meaning: Taking ~ as a trigger / using ~ as a chance
n2g014.explanation: Describes an event that became the trigger or turning point for a change.
n2g014.example: Using this accident as a trigger, safety measures were strengthened.

n2g015.explanation: Used to say that even though reason A exists, conclusion B doesn't necessarily follow.
n2g015.example: Just because you have money doesn't mean you're happy.

n2g016.meaning: As soon as / depending on / up to
n2g016.explanation: Verb stem + 次第 means "as soon as done." Noun + 次第 means "depending on."
n2g016.example: We will depart as soon as preparations are complete.

n2g017.meaning: Although / even though (but the result is contrary)
n2g017.explanation: Concedes a fact in the first clause but introduces a contrasting or disappointing reality.
n2g017.example: Although I studied, I failed the exam.

n2g018.explanation: Expresses that as one thing changes, another thing changes proportionally alongside it.
n2g018.example: Along with economic growth, the standard of living rose.

n2g019.explanation: Formal equivalent of で when indicating a place, situation, or field of activity.
n2g019.example: In modern society, information is extremely important.

n2g020.explanation: Expresses a standpoint or perspective from which something is evaluated.
n2g020.example: For children, play is important learning.

n1g001.explanation: Very formal expression meaning regardless of the nature or content of something.
n1g001.example: Regardless of the result, I will do my best.

n1g002.meaning: With / by means of / as of (a time)
n1g002.explanation: Has two meanings: (1) by means of something, (2) as of a certain point in time (formal announcement).
n1g002.example: As of today, this store will close.

n1g003.meaning: Unique to / only possible with / characteristic of
n1g003.explanation: Expresses that something is exclusively characteristic of or only possible because of a particular subject.
n1g003.example: There is a culture unique to Japan.

n1g004.explanation: Expresses that something meets the required standard or is worthy of a certain treatment.
n1g004.example: He is a person worthy of trust.

n1g005.meaning: Because of the special circumstance that ~ / given that ~
n1g005.explanation: Used when a special or unusual circumstance causes a particular result. The situation is noteworthy.
n1g005.example: Given that it was a three-day weekend, tourist spots were very crowded.

n1g006.meaning: Starting with ~ / beginning with ~ (as the first of many)
n1g006.explanation: Describes the first event in a series that triggers subsequent similar events.
n1g006.example: Starting with the Tokyo performance, the nationwide tour began.

n1g007.meaning: When it comes to ~ / once you become ~ (implying high expectations)
n1g007.explanation: Expresses that at a certain high level or in a certain special position, certain things naturally follow.
n1g007.example: When you become a company president, responsibility also becomes great.

n1g008.explanation: Even though a certain condition exists, the result is contrary to expectation. Very formal.
n1g008.example: Even a professional can fail sometimes.

n1g009.meaning: Cannot help but / will definitely cause / will inevitably do
n1g009.explanation: Has two meanings: (1) something inevitably causes a reaction, (2) the speaker will definitely do something.
n1g009.example: This movie cannot help but move its viewers.

n1g010.meaning: Is nothing but / is precisely / is exactly
n1g010.explanation: Asserts that something is precisely and nothing other than what is stated. Strong affirmation.
n1g010.example: This success is nothing other than the team's effort.

n1g011.meaning: Once ~ happens (there's no going back) / if ~ then it's all over
n1g011.explanation: Once a certain action takes place, an irreversible or extreme consequence follows.
n1g011.example: Once you start talking to her, she won't stop for an hour.

n1g012.explanation: Classical prohibition form. Seen on signs and formal written rules.

n1g013.meaning: Cannot stop ~ing / sincerely / from the bottom of one's heart
n1g013.explanation: Expresses a deep, unceasing feeling such as hope, love, or admiration.
n1g013.example: I sincerely hope for your continued success.

n1g014.meaning: Even if not ~ at least / if not fully then at least partially
n1g014.explanation: Suggests settling for a lesser alternative when the ideal is not possible.
n1g014.example: If not every day, at least you should exercise once a week.

n1g015.meaning: Undaunted by / in spite of (adversity) / without being deterred by
n1g015.explanation: Expresses that someone faced difficulties without being deterred — showing bravery or resilience.
n1g015.example: Undaunted by the storm, the ship moved forward.

n1g016.explanation: Formal equivalent of〜だけでなく. Used in written Japanese and formal speech.
n1g016.example: They are active not only domestically but also abroad.

n1g017.meaning: In accordance with / based on / in line with
n1g017.explanation: Indicates acting or thinking in direct accordance with rules, facts, or reality.
n1g017.example: Deal with it in accordance with the law.

n1g018.meaning: As soon as / no sooner than (frustrating repetition)
n1g018.explanation: Expresses frustration that as soon as one thing is done, the opposite immediately happens again.
n1g018.example: No sooner do I tidy up than the children make a mess again.

n1g019.explanation: Used to introduce a topic about someone or something that the speaker is exasperated or dissatisfied with.
n1g019.example: When it comes to my son, he doesn't study at all.

n1g020.explanation: Classical and formal expression of cause and reason. Literary equivalent of から or ので.
n1g020.example: Due to youth, mistakes were made.

n5l001.title: Greetings & Self-Introduction
n5l001.description: Learn essential Japanese greetings and how to introduce yourself.
n5l001.culturalNote: In Japan, bowing while greeting is customary. The depth of the bow reflects the level of respect.
dialogue: Hello! Nice to meet you. I am Tanaka.
Nice to meet you. I am Yamada. Please treat me well.
Likewise, please treat me well.

n5l002.title: Numbers & Counting
n5l002.description: Learn Japanese numbers from 1 to 10,000 and basic counters.
n5l002.culturalNote: Japanese has multiple counter systems depending on what is being counted.
dialogue: How many apples will you buy?
I will buy three.

n5l003.title: Family Members
n5l003.description: Learn vocabulary for family members in Japanese, including humble and honorific forms.
n5l003.culturalNote: Japanese uses different words for your own family (humble) vs. someone else's family (honorific). ちち = my father; おとうさん = your/someone's father.
dialogue: How many people are in your family?
There are four of us. I have a father, mother, and younger sister.
That's nice. I am an only child.

n5l004.title: Daily Routine & Time
n5l004.description: Learn to talk about daily activities and express time in Japanese.
n5l004.culturalNote: Japan uses both the 12-hour and 24-hour clock. Train schedules and official times often use the 24-hour format.
dialogue: What time do you wake up every morning?
I wake up at six. Then I take a shower and eat breakfast.
What time is school from and until?
It is from 8:30 until 3:00.

n5l005.title: Food & Ordering at a Restaurant
n5l005.description: Learn food vocabulary and how to order food at a Japanese restaurant.
n5l005.culturalNote: いただきます is said before eating, expressing gratitude. ごちそうさまでした is said after eating, thanking the cook or host.
dialogue: Welcome. What will you have?
One ramen and two gyoza please.
What would you like to drink?
Green tea please.

n4l001.title: Giving & Receiving (てあげる / てもらう / てくれる)
n4l001.description: Master the complex system of giving and receiving in Japanese.
n4l001.culturalNote: The direction of giving/receiving is crucial in Japanese. Using the wrong form can sound unnatural or even rude.
dialogue: Tanaka carried my bags for me.
That's kind. Did you have the teacher teach you?
Yes, I had the teacher teach me. It was very helpful.

n4l002.title: Causative & Passive Forms
n4l002.description: Learn how to make someone do something, and how to express being acted upon.
n4l002.culturalNote: The causative-passive form (させられる) often carries a nuance of being forced to do something against one's will.
dialogue: I was made to work overtime by the manager.
That must have been tough. I made my child eat vegetables.

n4l003.title: Expressing Conditions (〜ば / 〜たら / 〜と / 〜なら)
n4l003.description: Master the four conditional forms in Japanese and when to use each one.
n4l003.culturalNote: と is for natural/automatic consequences. たら is most versatile. ば is often for hypotheticals. なら is for advice based on new information.
dialogue: If you have time, shall we go see a movie?
When work finishes, I'll contact you.
If you're going to Tokyo, you should go to Sky Tree.

n4l004.title: Expressing Hearsay & Appearance (〜そう / 〜らしい / 〜ようだ)
n4l004.description: Learn how to express what things seem like and what you've heard.
n4l004.culturalNote: 〜そうだ has two completely different meanings depending on conjugation: verb-stem + そうだ = looks like; plain form + そうだ = hearsay.
dialogue: According to the news, it seems it will snow tomorrow.
Really? Looking at the sky, it certainly does seem cloudy.
It seems like Tanaka caught a cold.

n4l005.title: Making Requests & Giving Permission
n4l005.description: Learn polite ways to make requests and ask for or give permission.
n4l005.culturalNote: Politeness levels matter greatly in Japanese. Using too casual a form with a superior can be seen as disrespectful.
dialogue: Excuse me, is it alright if I open the window?
Yes, please go ahead. But since the air conditioning is on, please just a little.
Understood. Could you help me a bit?

n3l001.title: Expressing Reason & Cause (〜ため / 〜せいで / 〜おかげで)
n3l001.description: Learn nuanced ways to express reasons and causes, including blame and gratitude.
n3l001.culturalNote: おかげで implies positive outcome; せいで implies negative outcome. Using them incorrectly can seem sarcastic.
dialogue: It is thanks to the teacher that I passed the exam.
On the contrary, because of my poor health, I couldn't concentrate on the exam.
For next year too, let's prepare more.

n3l002.title: Expressing Contrast (〜のに / 〜くせに / 〜一方)
n3l002.description: Express contrast and unexpected results using various conjunctions.
n3l002.culturalNote: くせに is stronger and more critical than のに. It implies the speaker thinks the subject should know better.
dialogue: Even though I studied so much, I ended up failing the exam.
Despite knowing, he is pretending not to know.
While cities are convenient, on the other hand they lack nature.

n3l003.title: Potential, Desire & Necessity
n3l003.description: Express ability, desires, and necessity using various grammatical forms.
n3l003.culturalNote: べきだ expresses a moral obligation or advice; なければならない is a stronger, more external obligation.
dialogue: He is always wanting new games.
For your health, you should eat more vegetables.
You're right. We need to exercise every day.

n3l004.title: Quotation & Reported Speech
n3l004.description: Learn how to report what others said, thought, or heard.
n3l004.culturalNote: Japanese reported speech does not always change tense like English does. Context and time expressions carry tense information.
dialogue: According to Tanaka, it seems a new cafe opened near the station.
Yamada said they are going on a trip next week.
I heard from the manager that the meeting has been postponed.

n3l005.title: Expressing Change & Transformation
n3l005.description: Learn how to express gradual or sudden changes in state.
n3l005.culturalNote: てくる implies a change coming toward the present from the past; ていく implies a change going away into the future.
dialogue: After studying Japanese, I became able to understand the news.
Recently, the number of people who write letters has decreased.
Technology will continue to develop from here on.

n2l001.title: Formal Written Japanese
n2l001.description: Learn the key differences between spoken and written Japanese and formal expression patterns.
n2l001.culturalNote: Business Japanese (ビジネス日本語) has its own set of expressions and formulas. Keigo (敬語) — honorific language — is essential in professional settings.
dialogue: Dear Sir/Madam, I hope this letter finds you in good health and spirits.
Regarding this matter, we kindly request your confirmation.

n2l002.title: Keigo — Honorific Language Deep Dive
n2l002.description: Master sonkeigo (respectful), kenjougo (humble), and teineigo (polite) forms.
n2l002.culturalNote: Keigo is fundamental to Japanese professional life. Mistakes in keigo can cause significant social friction in formal settings.
dialogue: The manager is currently out.
Is Tanaka-sama available?
Could you please wait a moment?

n2l003.title: Complex Sentence Structures
n2l003.description: Build complex, multi-clause sentences using advanced connectives.
n2l003.culturalNote: 〜以上は and 〜からには both mean "now that / since" but 以上は is slightly more formal.
dialogue: Now that you have decided to do it, you must persevere until the end.
Although I want to study abroad, there is also the matter of money.
Although I applied, I have not yet been able to confirm the details.

n2l004.title: Reading News & Media Japanese
n2l004.description: Learn vocabulary and structures commonly used in Japanese news and media.
n2l004.culturalNote: News Japanese often uses passive voice and nominalizations. The style is dense and omits particles more frequently than conversational Japanese.
dialogue: According to the government's announcement, new economic measures are expected to be implemented from next month.
Along with the rise in prices, concerns are growing about the impact on household budgets.

n2l005.title: Expressing Degree & Extent
n2l005.description: Express degree, extent, and limits using advanced grammatical patterns.
n2l005.culturalNote: 〜だけあって acknowledges that a result is natural given a person's background or effort. It always has a positive or expected nuance.
dialogue: As expected of someone who works hard, her grades are very good.
As long as you are healthy, you can do anything else.
There is nobody who works as hard as him.

n1l001.title: Classical Japanese Elements in Modern Japanese
n1l001.description: Understand classical Japanese grammar patterns that survive in formal modern Japanese.
n1l001.culturalNote: Classical Japanese (文語/古文) appears in proverbs, set phrases, legal texts, formal literature, and signage. N1 candidates must recognize these patterns.
dialogue: If you try, you will succeed; if you do not try, nothing will be achieved.
More haste, less speed. (lit. If in a hurry, take the roundabout way.)
No entry for unauthorized persons.

n1l002.title: Nuanced Expressions of Emotion & Psychology
n1l002.description: Express subtle emotions and psychological states with precision.
n1l002.culturalNote: These expressions appear frequently in formal speeches, literary works, essays, and business correspondence. They convey deep sincerity.
dialogue: I could not help but be surprised at his reckless behavior.
I sincerely and endlessly hope for your health and development.
Knowing it, I couldn't help but say it.

n1l003.title: Logical & Academic Discourse
n1l003.description: Master the language of academic papers, debates, and logical argumentation.
n1l003.culturalNote: Japanese academic writing heavily uses noun-heavy structures, passive voice, and hedging expressions. Direct assertions are often softened.
dialogue: Based on these research results, I propose a new hypothesis.
The opponent's argument is not based on the facts.
This phenomenon can be considered to originate from economic disparities.

n1l004.title: Four-Character Idioms (四字熟語)
n1l004.description: Learn essential four-character compound words derived from Chinese classics.
n1l004.culturalNote: 四字熟語 are an important part of Japanese literary and formal culture. Many originate from Chinese classics (漢文) and Buddhist teachings.
dialogue: Her ability to adapt to situations is truly wonderful.
After repeating trial and error, a solution was finally found.
That's exactly killing two birds with one stone!

n1l005.title: Political, Legal & Economic Vocabulary
n1l005.description: Build vocabulary for understanding Japanese news, law, and economic discourse.
n1l005.culturalNote: The ability to understand NHK news broadcasts and read newspaper articles is a practical benchmark for N1 level Japanese.
dialogue: Based on the provisions of the constitution, a new law was enacted.
Against the backdrop of a declining birthrate, a review of immigration policy is being called for.
From an economic perspective, this policy is considered effective.

n4_g016.meaning: Passive voice (be done by someone / suffer from action)
n4_g016.explanation: Used when the subject receives an action from another person. In Japanese, 'suffering passive' (迷惑の受身) is often used when an action negatively affects the speaker.

n4_g017.explanation: Expresses making someone do something (force) or letting someone do something (permission).
n4_g017.example: Mother made my little brother eat vegetables.

n4_g018.meaning: Causative-Passive (be forced / made to do against one's will)
n4_g018.explanation: Combines causative and passive to express being coerced or forced into doing something you did not want to do.
n4_g018.example: I was forced to drink alcohol.

n4_g019.meaning: To finish completely / to do regretfully or accidentally
n4_g019.explanation: Has two distinct nuances: 1) Complete completion of an action, and 2) Regret or dismay over an unintended result.
n4_g019.example: I finished all of my homework completely.

n4_g020.meaning: Do something in advance / prepare ahead / leave as is
n4_g020.explanation: Indicates doing an action beforehand in preparation for the future, or leaving a current state undisturbed.
n4_g020.example: I will book the hotel in advance before the trip.

n4_g021.meaning: Try doing something to see what it's like
n4_g021.explanation: Used when attempting an action to test or experience the result.
n4_g021.example: I want to try eating Japanese natto.

n4_g022.meaning: Has been done intentionally (and the state remains)
n4_g022.explanation: Used with transitive verbs to show that someone intentionally performed an action and its result currently persists.
n4_g022.example: Names are written on the blackboard.

n4_g023.meaning: Easy to do / hard to do
n4_g023.explanation: Attached to the verb stem (masu-stem). Turns the verb into an i-adjective describing ease or difficulty.
n4_g023.example: This pen is very easy to write with.

n4_g024.explanation: Indicates doing an action or having a quality beyond a desirable or normal limit.

n4_g025.meaning: Might / may / possibly (50% or less certainty)
n4_g025.explanation: Expresses conjecture with lower probability than でしょう/だろう. In casual speech, contracted to かも.

n4_g026.meaning: Should be / supposed to be (strong expectation based on facts)
n4_g026.explanation: Expresses a high degree of confidence that something should happen based on logical reasoning or reliable facts.
n4_g026.example: Mr. Tanaka should have arrived already.

n4_g027.explanation: Used to declare one's own intention or decision. Not usually used to ask superiors about their plans.
n4_g027.example: I plan to go to Japan next year.

n4_g028.meaning: I heard that ~ / they say that ~ (hearsay)
n4_g028.explanation: Conveys information heard from another source without personal conjecture.
n4_g028.example: I heard it will snow tomorrow.

n4_g029.meaning: Not only... but also... / and what's more (listing reasons)
n4_g029.explanation: Lists two or more reasons or states that lead to a conclusion.
n4_g029.example: This restaurant is cheap, delicious, and always crowded.

n4_g030.explanation: The most flexible conditional in Japanese. Expresses 'if X happens' or 'when X is finished, then Y'.
n4_g030.example: When you arrive at the station, please call me.

n3_g016.meaning: There is no way that ~ / It is impossible that ~
n3_g016.explanation: Expresses a strong conviction that something is completely impossible based on reason or evidence.
n3_g016.example: There is no way he would tell a lie.

n3_g017.meaning: Cannot afford to / must not / cannot bring oneself to do
n3_g017.explanation: Expresses that one cannot do an action due to moral, social, or psychological reasons, even if one wants to.
n3_g017.example: Since there is an important meeting tomorrow, I cannot afford to take a day off.

n3_g018.meaning: Must be / bound to be / definitely is
n3_g018.explanation: Expresses strong, intuitive certainty without doubt.
n3_g018.example: The culprit must definitely be him.

n3_g019.explanation: Expresses that the outcome is surprising given the premise or standard.
n3_g019.example: Considering its price, this dish is very delicious.

n3_g020.meaning: Even though / despite the fact that (expressing blame/criticism)
n3_g020.explanation: Used like のに, but carries a strong tone of criticism, irritation, or contempt. Subject of both clauses must be the same.
n3_g020.example: Even though he doesn't say anything himself, he does nothing but complain.

n3_g021.explanation: Expresses that whenever event A occurs, event B always follows.
n3_g021.example: Every time I hear this song, I remember my student days.

n3_g022.meaning: While doing A, take the opportunity to also do B
n3_g022.explanation: Indicates doing a secondary action B while in the middle of performing primary action A.
n3_g022.example: While out for a walk, I mailed the letter.

n3_g023.meaning: Right in the middle of (an action unexpectedly interrupted)
n3_g023.explanation: Emphasizes that something unexpected happened exactly while an ongoing action was taking place.
n3_g023.example: Right in the middle of a meal, the phone rang.

n3_g024.meaning: Just as soon as ~ / the moment that ~ (instant surprise)
n3_g024.explanation: Expresses that immediately after action A occurred, an unexpected situation B took place.
n3_g024.example: The moment I opened the window, a strong wind rushed in.

n3_g025.explanation: Expresses gratitude for a positive result brought about by someone or something.
n3_g025.example: Thanks to the teacher, I was able to pass the exam.

n2g021.meaning: On the occasion of / prior to / when doing (formal)
n2g021.explanation: Formal expression used when beginning an important, official, or special event.
n2g021.example: On the occasion of launching the new enterprise, we made meticulous plans.

n2g022.meaning: Taking the opportunity of / as a turning point / prompted by
n2g022.explanation: Indicates that an event served as the catalyst or turning point for a significant positive or historical change.
n2g022.example: With the Olympics as a catalyst, redevelopment of the city progressed.

n2g023.meaning: Regardless of / irrespective of / without distinction of
n2g023.explanation: Indicates that a condition applies universally, irrespective of differences such as age, gender, or nationality.
n2g023.example: Anyone can apply, regardless of whether they have experience.

n2g024.meaning: Cannot help but do / have no choice but to do
n2g024.explanation: Expresses having no alternative other than doing something, despite not wanting to.
n2g024.example: With this much evidence, one cannot help but admit the facts.

n2g025.meaning: Cannot do / difficult to do (polite professional refusal)
n2g025.explanation: Used in business and professional contexts to politely decline requests or state inability to comply.
n2g025.example: We are unfortunately unable to comply with your request.

n1g021.meaning: Even if / no matter who/what it may be
n1g021.explanation: Expresses that under no circumstances or conditions does the following statement change.
n1g021.example: No matter what the reason may be, violence is never permitted.

n1g022.meaning: As someone who is / in the position of (ideal duty)
n1g022.explanation: Describes the moral duty, dignity, or behavior expected of someone in a high, professional, or responsible role.
n1g022.example: A true leader must always keep the bigger picture in perspective.

n1g023.meaning: Be forced to / have no choice but to (due to unavoidable external circumstances)
n1g023.explanation: Expresses that an undesirable change or cessation of action was compelled by circumstances completely beyond one's control.
n1g023.example: Due to the typhoon, we were forced to cancel the event.

n1g024.meaning: Coupled with / combined with / together with
n1g024.explanation: Expresses that two factors mutually interact or combine to produce a heightened effect.
n1g024.example: Talent coupled with relentless effort won him the world championship.

n1g025.meaning: Extremely / knows no bounds / peak of
n1g025.explanation: Conveys an extreme degree of emotion or state, often regarding dangerous, rude, or regrettable matters.
n1g025.example: Such an irresponsible attitude is regrettable in the extreme.

n4_031.example: I will guide you around town.

n4_032.example: Please contact me when you arrive.

n4_033.example: I have an appointment with a friend.

n4_035.example: This grammar is a bit complicated.

n4_038.example: The scenery from the mountain is beautiful.

n4_039.example: Waking up early is a good habit.

n4_041.example: I am interested in Japanese culture.

n4_042.example: Please let me hear your opinion.

n4_043.example: I consulted the teacher about my future.

n4_045.example: The elevator is out of order.

n3_026.example: We are striving to improve our services.

n3_028.example: Let us protect the natural environment.

n3_029.example: Fulfill one's responsibility as a leader.

n3_031.example: Recovery of the global economy is expected.

n3_034.example: We achieved our target for this term.

n3_035.example: He is trusted by his peers.

n2_031.example: The government's new policy was announced.

n2_033.example: Do not forget consideration for those around you.

n1_031.example: His preeminent ability was highly evaluated.

n1_033.example: Submit an inquiry to the expert committee.

n1_034.example: Acutely feel the divergence between ideal and reality.

n5v062.example: I eat breakfast at 7 o'clock every morning.

n5v063.example: I went to eat lunch with a friend.

n5v065.example: Let's meet in front of the station.

n5v067.example: I wrote a letter to my mother.

n5v068.example: I forgot my wallet at home.

n5v070.example: It is raining, so I will take an umbrella.

n5v071.example: Please take off your shoes at the entrance.

n5v074.example: I listen carefully with my ears.

n5v075.example: I wash my hands before eating.

n5v076.example: My legs are tired from walking a lot.

n5v079.example: There is a cat in the garden.

n5l006.title: Asking for Directions
n5l006.description: Learn how to navigate Japanese cities and ask for directions politely.
n5l006.culturalNote: Japanese police boxes (交番, kouban) are prominent throughout cities and will happily provide directions with maps.
dialogue: Excuse me, where is the station?
Go straight along this street and turn right.
Thank you very much!

n5l007.title: Shopping & Asking Prices
n5l007.description: Learn how to ask for prices, specify items, and purchase goods in stores.
n5l007.culturalNote: When paying in Japan, you place your money into a small plastic or metallic tray (カルトン) on the counter rather than handing it directly.
dialogue: Excuse me, how much is this umbrella?
It is 1,000 yen.
Well then, I will take this please.

n5l008.title: Ordering at Restaurants
n5l008.description: Master ordering delicious Japanese food, asking for water, and requesting the bill.
n5l008.culturalNote: Saying ごちそうさまでした (Gochisousama deshita) when leaving a restaurant expresses heartfelt gratitude for the meal.
dialogue: Excuse me, could I get some water?
Yes, certainly.
Also, one bowl of ramen, please.

n5l009.title: Hobbies & Leisure
n5l009.description: Talk about your favorite hobbies, sports, music, and weekend activities.
n5l009.culturalNote: In Japan, sharing hobbies (趣味) is one of the most common icebreakers when meeting new classmates or colleagues.
dialogue: What is your hobby?
Watching movies and listening to music.
What kind of movies do you like?

n5l010.title: Travel & Vacation Plans
n5l010.description: Learn how to discuss upcoming trips, hotel stays, and vacation dates.
n5l010.culturalNote: Giving おみやげ (omiyage - souvenir gifts, usually regional snacks) to friends and coworkers after traveling is an essential social norm.
dialogue: Did you go anywhere over the weekend?
I went to Kyoto and took lots of photos.
How nice! Did you also buy souvenirs?

n4l006.title: Giving and Receiving Favors
n4l006.description: Master the nuance of doing things for others and receiving favors using てあげる, てくれる, and てもらう.
n4l006.culturalNote: In Japanese culture, acknowledging who initiated a favor preserves harmonious social distance and gratitude.
dialogue: That luggage looks heavy. Shall I carry it for you?
Thank you very much! That is a great help.

n4l007.title: Expressing Completion & Regret
n4l007.description: Express total completion and unintentional mistakes using 〜てしまう.
n4l007.culturalNote: 〜てしまう expresses an empathetic vulnerability, signaling to listeners that an error was not malicious.
dialogue: What happened? You don't look well.
I accidentally left my umbrella on the train.

n4l008.title: Conditionals in Daily Conversation
n4l008.description: Learn the differences between 〜たら, 〜ば, 〜なら, and 〜と in real-world scenarios.
n4l008.culturalNote: 〜と is strictly for natural constants and machine consequences (press this button and change comes out).
dialogue: If the weather is good tomorrow, shall we go to the beach?
Sounds great! If it rains, let's make it an art museum instead.

n4l009.title: Potential and Abilities
n4l009.description: Learn how to describe what you can and cannot do using potential verb conjugations.
n4l009.culturalNote: Potential verbs mark their object with が instead of を in standard Japanese (e.g. 寿司が食べられる).
dialogue: Can you read Japanese newspapers?
I can still only read a few kanji.

n4l010.title: Workplace Requests & Keigo Basics
n4l010.description: Learn foundational honorific and humble expressions for office and retail environments.
n4l010.culturalNote: Keigo reflects humility towards clients and elders while maintaining professional boundaries.
dialogue: Director, could you please check this document?
Understood. I will look at it later.

n3l006.title: Explaining Circumstances and Nuances
n3l006.description: Express complex reasoning and clarify misunderstandings using 〜わけだ and 〜わけではない.
n3l006.culturalNote: 〜わけだ shows that you have synthesized the facts and empathetically understand the situation.
dialogue: Apparently he suddenly returned to his home country.
I heard his mother fell ill. So that is why he hurried back.

n3l007.title: Contrasts and Surprising Outcomes
n3l007.description: Compare expectations with reality using 〜わりに and 〜くせに.
n3l007.culturalNote: Nuance matters: 〜くせに is strictly derogatory and should never be used toward customers or superiors.
dialogue: Even though this PC was cheap, it is really fast!
It has a reputation for great performance considering the price.

n3l008.title: Business Meetings & Problem Solving
n3l008.description: Communicate project updates, report delays, and offer collaborative solutions.
n3l008.culturalNote: The Japanese business reporting framework Horenso (報告・連絡・相談) is vital in team dynamics.
dialogue: I have a report regarding the project's progress.
Is there a risk that we might miss the delivery deadline?

n3l009.title: Healthcare & Clinical Visits
n3l009.description: Describe medical symptoms, fever, allergy reactions, and medication schedules accurately.
n3l009.culturalNote: In Japan, pharmacies require an official doctor's prescription (処方箋, shohousen) for most clinical treatments.
dialogue: I have felt a bit feverish since yesterday, and my throat hurts unbearably.
Don't push yourself; take your medicine and get some rest.

n3l010.title: Weather Forecasts & Natural Disasters
n3l010.description: Understand news reports on typhoons, earthquakes, evacuation warnings, and seasonal weather.
n3l010.culturalNote: Japan is world-renowned for disaster preparedness drills (防災訓練) held regularly across schools and workplaces.
dialogue: A large typhoon is approaching, with risk of storm conditions starting tonight.
Let us confirm the evacuation shelters in advance.

n2l006.title: Executive Presentations & Public Speaking
n2l006.description: Structure formal business pitches, introduce project proposals, and address stakeholder questions.
n2l006.culturalNote: Japanese business presentations follow the Ki-Shou-Ten-Ketsu or Premise-Analysis-Proposal flow.
dialogue: On the occasion of today's presentation, I will make a proposal based on recent market trends.
Very interesting. Please share the specific implementation timeline.

n2l007.title: Contract Negotiations & Corporate Inquiries
n2l007.description: Master diplomatic business negotiations, formal concession requests, and contractual terms.
n2l007.culturalNote: Directly saying "No" (いいえ) in Japanese negotiations is avoided; phrases like 応じかねます or 検討いたします are standard.
dialogue: We sincerely apologize, but we are unable to comply with the proposed delivery date.
Is that so? In that case, we have no choice but to reconsider.

n2l008.title: Editorial Reading & Media Discourse
n2l008.description: Analyze newspaper editorials, op-eds, and economic columns with sophisticated grammatical connectors.
n2l008.culturalNote: JLPT N2 reading comprehension relies heavily on recognizing logical shift markers like 一方で and 反面.
dialogue: While digitalization advances, privacy protection is gradually becoming an urgent challenge.
To enjoy the benefits of technological innovation, establishing sound regulations is nothing less than essential.

n2l009.title: Demographics & Societal Transformations
n2l009.description: Discuss sociological changes, birthrate dynamics, regional revitalization, and workforce diversification.
n2l009.culturalNote: Regional revitalization (地方創生, chihou sousei) is one of the highest priority socioeconomic initiatives in modern Japan.
dialogue: Concurrently with the aging population, the expansion of social security costs is raising concern.
Building sustainable local communities across the entire nation is indeed urgent.

n2l010.title: Customer Relations & Crisis Management
n2l010.description: Handle customer grievances, issue public apologies, and communicate corrective measures with maximum etiquette.
n2l010.culturalNote: Formal Japanese corporate apologies follow a codified protocol emphasizing restitution, humility, and root-cause remediation.
dialogue: Regarding our recent oversight, we offer our most humble apologies.
Going forward, please enforce thorough preventive measures so this never occurs again.

n1l006.title: Classical Nuance in Formal Modern Prose
n1l006.description: Decipher classical literary particles, archaic verbs, and historic grammatical patterns embedded in official declarations.
n1l006.culturalNote: Classical grammatical markers like 〜たるもの lend an elevated moral authority and gravity to Japanese statecraft.
dialogue: Those who are legislators entrusted by the people must cast aside self-interest and serve the public good.
Indeed so. Corruption is an unpardonable act.

n1l007.title: Academic Research & Peer Review Discourse
n1l007.description: Engage in academic methodology, critique scientific hypotheses, and defend experimental findings.
n1l007.culturalNote: Japanese academic publications require rigorous modesty (謙譲) coupled with indisputable empirical substantiation.
dialogue: Meticulous data analysis coupled with logical inference lends this paper immense persuasive power.
No matter what counter-arguments may arise, overturning these empirical results will be difficult.

n1l008.title: Corporate Governance & Strategic Mergers
n1l008.description: Debate shareholder rights, antitrust compliance, corporate acquisition, and executive fiduciary duties.
n1l008.culturalNote: Japan's revised Corporate Governance Code places heavy emphasis on independent outside directors and capital efficiency.
dialogue: Due to intensifying market competition, we were forced into divesting unprofitable divisions.
As a board director, actions impairing shareholder value are unpardonable.

n1l009.title: Jurisprudence & Constitutional Philosophy
n1l009.description: Analyze legal precedents, judicial interpretations of constitutional rights, and legal equity.
n1l009.culturalNote: The Supreme Court of Japan (最高裁判所) serves as the ultimate arbiter of constitutional interpretation.
dialogue: In accordance with changing times, flexible application of constitutional interpretation is being debated.
It is essential to uphold the rule of law while safeguarding the fundamental human rights of citizens.

n1l010.title: Literary Critique & Aesthetic Philosophy
n1l010.description: Explore the aesthetic concepts of 物の哀れ (mono no aware), 幽玄 (yuugen), and わび・さび (wabi-sabi) in classical and modern prose.
n1l010.culturalNote: Mono no aware (物の哀れ) captures the gentle sadness of impermanence, famously epitomized in The Tale of Genji (源氏物語).
dialogue: The sense of transience that permeates classical literature can truly be called the crystallization of an aesthetic sensibility unique to Japan.
Even the simple sentiment of lamenting the falling cherry blossoms speaks to that profound spirituality.
